passage: Oceanographers studying coastal ecosystems have observed a steady rise in the number of harmful algal blooms over the last several decades. These blooms occur when certain algae species reproduce rapidly, often turning the water red or brown and releasing toxins that can harm marine life. Although some growth occurs naturally, scientists attribute the recent increase to nutrient runoff from agriculture and urban development. Fertilizers rich in nitrogen and phosphorus enter waterways during heavy rains, providing algae with an abundant food source. Warmer ocean temperatures also accelerate growth by creating favorable conditions for these species. The consequences can be severe: fish die-offs, shellfish contamination, and temporary closures of coastal industries such as tourism and fishing. In response, researchers are developing early-warning models that combine satellite imagery with water-quality sensors to predict bloom formation before it spreads widely.
